questions.prompt: Find the cofactor $A_{21}$ of the element $4$ in $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -5 & 6 \\ 3 & 5 & 2 \end{vmatrix}$.
questions.solution: Delete Row 2 and Column 1 to get $M_{21} = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 5 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = (3)(2) - (-2)(5) = 6 + 10 = 16$. Then $A_{21} = (-1)^{2+1} M_{21} = -16$.

questions.solution: Use $R_1 \to R_1 + 7R_3$ and $R_4 \to R_4 + 3R_3$ to clear Column 4 except at $(3,4)$: Column 4 becomes $(0, 0, -1, 0)^T$. Expanding along Column 4 with sign $(-1)^{3+4} = -1$ gives $-(-1)\begin{vmatrix} 45 & 30 & 19 \\ -1 & -4 & -3 \\ 20 & 11 & 6 \end{vmatrix} = 96$.

questions.prompt: The value of the determinant $\begin{vmatrix} 5^2 & 5^3 & 5^4 \\ 5^3 & 5^4 & 5^5 \\ 5^4 & 5^6 & 5^7 \end{vmatrix}$ is:
questions.solution: Factor $5^2$ from $R_1$ and $5^3$ from $R_2$: both Row 1 and Row 2 become $(1,\; 5,\; 5^2)$. By Property (iii), two identical rows imply the determinant equals $0$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Objective Questions, Q1

questions.prompt: If $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 \\ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 \end{vmatrix} = 5$, then the value of its cofactor determinant $\begin{vmatrix} A_1 & B_1 & C_1 \\ A_2 & B_2 & C_2 \\ A_3 & B_3 & C_3 \end{vmatrix}$ is:
questions.solution: Multiplying $\Delta$ row-by-row by its cofactor determinant produces a diagonal determinant with entries $\Delta, \Delta, \Delta$, whose value is $\Delta^3$. Hence $\Delta \cdot \Delta_{\text{cof}} = \Delta^3 \implies \Delta_{\text{cof}} = \Delta^2 = 5^2 = 25$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Objective Questions, Q2 (cf. Example 64)

questions.prompt: If $1, \omega, \omega^2$ are the cube roots of unity (with $n$ not a multiple of $3$), then $\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & \omega^n & \omega^{2n} \\ \omega^n & \omega^{2n} & 1 \\ \omega^{2n} & 1 & \omega^n \end{vmatrix}$ equals:
questions.solution: Apply $C_1 \to C_1 + C_2 + C_3$. Every entry in Column 1 becomes $1 + \omega^n + \omega^{2n}$, which equals $0$ whenever $n$ is not a multiple of $3$ (and if $n$ is a multiple of $3$, all entries are $1$ so rows are identical and $\Delta = 0$ as well). Thus $\Delta = 0$ for every integer $n$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Objective Questions, Q4 (cf. Example 20)

questions.prompt: Using pivotal condensation (or row operations), evaluate $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 & 2 & 5 \\ 6 & 1 & 7 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 9 & 2 \end{vmatrix}$.
questions.solution: With pivot $a_1 = 1$ ($n = 4$), $D = \dfrac{1}{1^2}\begin{vmatrix} 4-6 & 2-3 & 5-9 \\ 1-12 & 7-6 & 1-18 \\ 3-8 & 9-4 & 2-12 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} -2 & -1 & -4 \\ -11 & 1 & -17 \\ -5 & 5 & -10 \end{vmatrix}$. Condensing again with pivot $-2$: $D = \dfrac{1}{-2}\begin{vmatrix} -2-11 & 34-44 \\ -10-5 & 20-20 \end{vmatrix} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\begin{vmatrix} -13 & -10 \\ -15 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -\dfrac{1}{2}(0 - 150) = 75$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Exercise 4.6, Q4

questions.prompt: Which statement is ALWAYS true for skew-symmetric determinants?

options.label: A
options.text: Every skew-symmetric determinant of even order equals zero.

options.label: B
options.text: Every skew-symmetric determinant of odd order vanishes, and every even-order one is a perfect square.

options.label: C
options.text: The leading diagonal of a skew-symmetric determinant consists of all $1$s.

options.label: D
options.text: Interchanging two rows of a skew-symmetric determinant leaves its sign unchanged.

questions.solution: By §4.11, factoring $-1$ from each of $n$ columns and transposing gives $\Delta = (-1)^n \Delta$. For odd $n$, $\Delta = -\Delta \implies \Delta = 0$. For even $n$, $\Delta$ is always a perfect square (Property 2).

questions.prompt: Using determinants, find the area (in square units) of the triangle whose vertices are $(-2, 4)$, $(2, -6)$, and $(5, 4)$.
questions.solution: Form $\Delta = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{vmatrix} -2 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -6 & 1 \\ 5 & 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\right|$. Apply $R_1 \to R_1 - R_3$: Row 1 becomes $(-7, 0, 0)$. Expanding along Row 1 gives $\dfrac{1}{2}|-7(-6 - 4)| = \dfrac{1}{2}|70| = 35\text{ sq. units}$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Exercise 4.7, Q2

questions.prompt: Find the value of $\alpha$ such that the points $(1, -5)$, $(-4, 5)$, and $(\alpha, 7)$ are collinear.
questions.solution: Collinearity requires $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -5 & 1 \\ -4 & 5 & 1 \\ \alpha & 7 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$. Apply $R_1 \to R_1 - R_2$ and $R_2 \to R_2 - R_3$: $\begin{vmatrix} 5 & -10 & 0 \\ -4 - \alpha & -2 & 0 \\ \alpha & 7 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0 \implies 5(-2) - (-10)(-4 - \alpha) = 0 \implies -10 - 40 - 10\alpha = 0 \implies \alpha = -5$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Exercise 4.7, Q6

questions.prompt: The homogeneous system $x + \alpha y = 0$, $y + \alpha z = 0$, $z + \alpha x = 0$ has infinitely many solutions when:
questions.solution: For nontrivial (infinitely many) solutions of a homogeneous system, $D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & \alpha & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & \alpha \\ \alpha & 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$. Expanding along Column 1 gives $1(1 - 0) + \alpha(\alpha^2 - 0) = 1 + \alpha^3 = 0$, whose unique real root is $\alpha = -1$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Objective Questions, Q11

questions.prompt: If the homogeneous system $x - ky - z = 0$, $kx - y - z = 0$, $x + y - z = 0$ has a non-zero solution, then the possible values of $k$ are:
questions.solution: Set $D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -k & -1 \\ k & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$. Apply $R_1 \to R_1 - R_3$ and $R_2 \to R_2 - R_3$: $\begin{vmatrix} 0 & -k - 1 & 0 \\ k - 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$. Expanding along Column 3 gives $(-1)\big(0 + (k+1)(k-1)\big) = 0 \implies k^2 - 1 = 0 \implies k = -1, 1$.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Objective Questions, Q12

questions.prompt: Find the value of $\lambda$ for which the system $2x - y - 2z = 2$, $x - 2y + z = -4$, $x + y + \lambda z = 4$ has no solution.
questions.solution: Compute $D = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 2(-2\lambda - 1) + 1(\lambda - 1) - 2(1 + 2) = -3\lambda - 9$. Setting $D = 0$ gives $\lambda = -3$. Checking $D_1$ at $\lambda = -3$: $D_1 = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 & -2 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & -3 \end{vmatrix} = 2(6 - 1) + 1(12 - 4) - 2(-4 + 8) = 10 + 8 - 8 = 10 \neq 0$, confirming inconsistency.
questions.source: H. K. Dass, Ch. 4, Objective Questions, Q13
